title: A Farmer's Daughter Died Because India's Biggest Medical Exam Was Cancelled. She Was Not the Last Victim.
excerpt: Akanksha Chaturvedi scored well on NEET. Then the paper leak happened. The re-exam broke her. Now scammers are selling fake papers to desperate families for ₹20 lakh.
body:
Akanksha Chaturvedi was expecting around 650 marks on the NEET-UG examination she took on May 3. She was among 22.05 lakh students who sat for India's single-window medical entrance test, and by every account, she had prepared well. Her father, Krishna Kumar Chaturvedi, a farmer in Madhya Pradesh's Mauganj district, had taken a ₹3 lakh loan through his Kisan Credit Card and moved to Nagpur to work as a cook while his daughter studied at a coaching institute.

Then the National Testing Agency cancelled the examination.

On May 12, the NTA announced that credible paper leak allegations had compromised the test. A re-exam was scheduled for June 21. For Akanksha, the news was not a fresh start. It was a collapse.

She left behind a handwritten note. "Mummy Papa, you believed your daughter would study and become a doctor. But I do not have the courage to take the NEET exam again. I have ruined both of you," she wrote. "There is no guarantee that I will perform well if I appear for the examination again."

## The scale of the failure

The NEET-UG 2026 paper leak is not a minor irregularity. The Rajasthan Police Special Operations Group reportedly found a "guess paper" containing more than 410 questions, of which approximately 120 appeared in the Biology and Chemistry sections of the actual examination. The Central Bureau of Investigation has registered an FIR and arrested 13 people so far. The CBI probe is expected to conclude by mid-June.

The cancellation affected every one of the 22 lakh students who took the exam. For many, the months of preparation represented the single largest financial and emotional investment their families had ever made. Coaching fees alone can run into lakhs of rupees — a crushing burden for families like the Chaturvedis who borrow against agricultural credit lines to fund their children's futures.

## The scammers moved in immediately

Within days of the re-exam announcement, a parallel economy of fraud materialized. The NTA has now referred to cybercrime authorities at least three Telegram groups that were openly advertising "leaked" re-exam papers for sale.

Journalists who investigated the networks found an elaborate operation. One channel operator, contacted by a Times of India reporter posing as a parent, quoted a price of ₹20 lakh. The arrangement was specific: pay a ₹50,000 token, meet in a Bengaluru office, leave the OMR answer sheets blank on exam day, and the network would ensure "the right answers are filled" for a guaranteed score of 620 or higher.

Another operator, identifying himself as a coaching institute faculty member in Delhi, claimed his network had purchased "half the paper" for ₹35 lakh, with the rest available closer to the exam date. He allegedly assured buyers that the network had "protection from influential individuals."

## The political fallout

Rahul Gandhi launched a sharp attack on Prime Minister Modi, saying an entire generation of young Indians is paying the price for how the education system has been handled over the past 12 years. Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan ordered the re-exam and CBI probe, and Defence Minister Rajnath Singh confirmed the Indian Air Force has been brought in to assist with logistics and security for the June 21 re-test.

## What the diaspora should understand

For NRIs whose families still navigate India's competitive examination system, the NEET crisis crystallizes a structural fear: that the institutions meant to ensure meritocratic access to medical education are not secure. The exam is the only gateway to approximately 108,000 MBBS seats across India. When it fails, there is no alternative path.

The re-exam is scheduled for June 21, with admit cards expected by June 14. The NTA has extended the exam window by 15 minutes and pushed the fee refund deadline to June 22. City intimation slips are expected this week.

None of that will bring Akanksha Chaturvedi back. And none of it addresses the question her suicide note forces: how many other students, in other small towns, from other farming families, are making the same calculation — that the system has already failed them, and another attempt is not worth the cost.
